front:
What does this program do, and why does it exit this way?
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
int main() {
    std::thread t([] { /* worker body omitted */ });
    std::cout << "main reaches end of scope without join\n";
}
back:
Headline: it aborts with std::terminate before the thread is ever joined.
Real output:
terminate called without an active exception
[exit: SIGABRT, shell status 134]

A joinable std::thread destroyed without join() or detach() calls std::terminate. The cout line never shows here: stdout was a pipe (fully buffered) and abort() does not flush it. Fix: join() or detach() explicitly, or use std::jthread (C++20), whose destructor requests stop and joins.
Interview trap: detach() makes the thread unobservable: you cannot wait for it, and an uncaught exception inside it terminates the program.

front:
Why does this not compile, and how do you fix it? Show the corrected code and its output.
#include <thread>
void bump(int& x) { x += 1; }
int main() {
    int x = 0;
    std::thread t(bump, x);
    t.join();
}
back:
Headline: std::thread decay-copies its arguments, so the function receives a temporary int, which cannot bind to int&.
Real first compiler error:
/usr/include/c++/13/bits/std_thread.h:157:72: error: static assertion failed: std::thread arguments must be invocable after conversion to rvalues

Fix: wrap the reference with std::ref (the copy becomes a std::reference_wrapper that binds to the original):
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
void bump(int& x) { x += 1; }
int main() {
    int x = 0;
    std::thread t(bump, std::ref(x));
    t.join();
    std::cout << x << "\n";
}

Real output:
1

Interview trap: passing a pointer copies the pointer, not the value, and the thread can then outlive the pointee.

front:
Two threads each run 1,000,000 iterations of ++counter on a plain global int. What is wrong, what does it print, and is the printed value evidence that the code is correct?
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
int counter = 0;
void work() { for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; ++i) ++counter; }
int main() {
    std::thread a(work), b(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << counter << "\n";
}
back:
Headline: this is a data race, so the program has undefined behaviour and no printed value proves it correct.
Real output at -O0:
1018401 , 1000000 , 1406027 (three runs at -O0)

Real output at -O2:
2000000 , 2000000 , 2000000 , 2000000 , 2000000 (five runs at -O2)

At -O2 GCC hoists the loop out of the global: the worker's whole loop compiles to addl $1000000, counter(%rip) followed by ret, so the race never happens in that build and the printed total is right. At -O0 the lost updates show. ThreadSanitizer reports: WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race.
Fix: a std::atomic counter (see the relaxed-counter card) or a mutex (next card).
Interview trap: 'it printed the right number in my test' is not evidence in C++. Use TSan, or check the optimised assembly.

front: A {{c1::data race}} is a pair of conflicting accesses to one memory location, not both atomic, that are not ordered by happens-before. It is {{c2::undefined behaviour}} in C++. Two relaxed atomic operations on the same object are {{c3::not a data race}}, but they order no other memory.
back: Relaxed atomics give atomicity and a single modification order for that one object. They do not publish other writes; for that you need release/acquire (see the memory-ordering chain).

front:
Fix the counter so the total is exact. Show the code and output, and say what the fix costs.
#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
int counter = 0;
std::mutex m;
void work() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; ++i) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m);
        ++counter;
    }
}
int main() {
    std::thread a(work), b(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << counter << "\n";
}
back:
Headline: protect the increment with std::mutex; std::lock_guard unlocks in its destructor, even on exceptions.
Real output:
2000000

Cost: each increment is a lock acquire and release. Uncontended this is a few atomic operations. When threads collide, the mutex word and the counter's cache line move between cores, and waiters can sleep in the kernel. The lock covers the whole loop body, so the threads run one at a time: there is no parallel speedup. The next card shows the standard fix.

front:
[Chain: MUTEX 1/3] Context: four threads each add the numbers 0 to 999,999 into one shared total, taking a mutex for every addition. What does the program print, is the naive version correct, and what is the design smell?
#include <cstdint>
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
std::mutex m;
std::uint64_t shared_total = 0;
void naive(std::uint64_t n) {
    for (std::uint64_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m);
        shared_total += i;
    }
}
void local(std::uint64_t n, std::uint64_t& out) {
    std::uint64_t acc = 0;
    for (std::uint64_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) acc += i;
    out = acc;
}
int main() {
    const std::uint64_t N = 1000000;
    const int T = 4;
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int k = 0; k < T; ++k) ts.emplace_back(naive, N);
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    std::cout << "naive total: " << shared_total << "\n";

    std::vector<std::uint64_t> parts(T, 0);
    std::vector<std::thread> ts2;
    for (int k = 0; k < T; ++k) ts2.emplace_back(local, N, std::ref(parts[k]));
    for (auto& t : ts2) t.join();
    std::uint64_t sum = 0;
    for (auto p : parts) sum += p;
    std::cout << "local total: " << sum << "\n";
}
back:
Headline: the total is correct: 4 times the sum 0..999,999 equals 1,999,998,000,000.
Real output:
naive total: 1999998000000
local total: 1999998000000

Design smell: there are 4,000,000 lock/unlock pairs, all on one shared variable, so the threads queue behind each other and the work is effectively serial. Count the synchronisation before counting the arithmetic. The local-accumulator version below does four synchronisations in total.
Interviewer follow-up: 'Which part of the loop is serial in this design, and what does that do to scaling?' (Answer on the next card.)

front: [Chain: MUTEX 2/3] Context: four threads, each doing 1,000,000 lock, add, unlock on one shared total (4,000,000 critical sections in all). Why is this not faster on four idle cores? Give the first-principles reasons.
back:
Headline: the critical section is essentially the whole loop, so the serial fraction is close to 1 and the mutex also adds coherence traffic.
1. Amdahl: with serial fraction s, the speedup on N cores is at most 1/s. Here s is close to 1, so the bound is close to 1.
2. Coherence traffic: each lock and unlock is an atomic read-modify-write on the mutex word, and the counter sits on the same or a nearby line. Ownership of that cache line moves between cores on every handoff.
3. Kernel waits: under contention, a waiter may sleep in the kernel (futex) and be woken later; the wake-up path costs far more than the increment.
Quantitative aside (approx.): if the critical section were 1 ns and the parallel work 100 ns per iteration, s = 1/101 and the Amdahl bound on 4 threads is 3.88. The lock is cheap only when the work outside it is large.
Interviewer follow-up: 'So what is the fix that keeps the mutex?' Keep the mutex for the rare shared update and do the frequent work privately.

front: [Chain: MUTEX 3/3] Context: the mutex version serialises every addition. Rewrite it so each thread accumulates into a local variable and touches shared state once, with the reduction after join. Show the key function, then say where this design still breaks.
back:
Fix: the accumulator stays in a register or on the stack, and each thread writes its result once:
void local(std::uint64_t n, std::uint64_t& out) {
    std::uint64_t acc = 0;
    for (std::uint64_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) acc += i;
    out = acc;
}

Real output:
local total: 1999998000000 (the local version, from the same run)

Joining the threads before reading parts gives a happens-before edge, so the main thread's plain reads are race-free.
Where it breaks: writing parts[k] inside the hot loop puts adjacent 8-byte slots on one 64-byte cache line (false sharing), so every write bounces the line between cores. Keep the accumulator local, or pad each slot to 64 bytes with alignas(64). Also, a parallel floating-point reduction depends on the order of additions, so fix the reduction order if results must be bit-reproducible.

front:
Thread 1 locks a then b, thread 2 locks b then a. Predict what this program does, why, and what the standard fix is.
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <mutex>
#include <thread>
std::mutex a, b;
int main() {
    std::thread t1([] {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> ga(a);
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(50));
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> gb(b);
    });
    std::thread t2([] {
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> gb(b);
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(50));
        std::lock_guard<std::mutex> ga(a);
    });
    t1.join();
    t2.join();
    std::cout << "both threads finished\n";
}
back:
Headline: it hangs. The program never prints its final line.
Real output:
(no output: the process was still running when the harness stopped it after 5 seconds)
The sleeps make the interleaving reliable: each thread holds one mutex and waits for the other, a circular wait. All four Coffman conditions hold (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait); breaking any one prevents the deadlock. Usually you break circular wait with a single lock call or a global lock order.
Fix: lock both in one call with std::scoped_lock (next card).
Interview trap: two std::lock_guard objects taken in one function, in different orders, is the bug. Two lock_guards in the same order are fine, but nothing enforces that across the codebase.

front: {{c1::std::lock_guard}} locks in its constructor and unlocks in its destructor, and cannot be unlocked early. {{c2::std::unique_lock}} can be unlocked and relocked and is the lock type that {{c3::std::condition_variable::wait}} requires. {{c4::std::scoped_lock}} takes one or more mutexes with deadlock avoidance.
back: Use lock_guard for a single short critical section, unique_lock when you need to unlock early or wait on a condition, and scoped_lock whenever you take more than one mutex.

front:
Both threads do 1,000,000 fetch_add(1, memory_order_relaxed) on one std::atomic. What does this print, and why is relaxed enough for a counter?
#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
std::atomic<long long> counter{0};
void work() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000000; ++i)
        counter.fetch_add(1, std::memory_order_relaxed);
}
int main() {
    std::thread a(work), b(work);
    a.join();
    b.join();
    std::cout << counter.load() << "\n";
    std::cout << std::atomic<long long>::is_always_lock_free << "\n";
}
back:
Headline: the count is exact, because the increments are atomic read-modify-write operations on one object.
Real output:
2000000
1
The second line is std::atomic<long long>::is_always_lock_free: 1 means no hidden mutex on this target. Relaxed guarantees atomicity and a single modification order for counter. It publishes no other data, and it does not need to: join() orders the workers' effects before main's read.
Interview trap: relaxed is fine for counters and statistics, but never for a flag that guards other data. That needs release/acquire.

front:
[Chain: MEMORDER 1/3] Context: a producer writes a plain int payload = 42 and then sets an atomic flag. A consumer spins until it sees the flag and reads payload. Which memory orders make this correct, and what does the program print?
#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
int payload = 0;
std::atomic<bool> ready{false};
int main() {
    std::thread producer([] {
        payload = 42;
        ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);
    });
    std::thread consumer([] {
        while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {}
        std::cout << payload << "\n";
    });
    producer.join();
    consumer.join();
}
back:
Headline: release store on the flag and acquire load on the consumer side.
Real output:
42
The release store makes all writes before it visible to any thread whose acquire load reads that value. That creates a happens-before edge, so the consumer's read of the plain int is ordered after the write and is not a data race.
Interviewer follow-up: 'Does the consumer need any ordering on the spin loop itself?' Yes: the acquire load is what gives the edge; a relaxed load of the same flag would not (next card).

front:
[Chain: MEMORDER 2/3] Context: the same producer and consumer, but both sides use memory_order_relaxed. Our run printed 42. Is the code correct? Give the evidence. 
#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
int payload = 0;
std::atomic<bool> ready{false};
int main() {
    std::thread producer([] {
        payload = 42;
        ready.store(true, std::memory_order_relaxed);
    });
    std::thread consumer([] {
        while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {}
        std::cout << payload << "\n";
    });
    producer.join();
    consumer.join();
}
back:
Headline: no. The output is not evidence of correctness.
Real output:
42

[ThreadSanitizer, -O1] WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race
Relaxed operations do not order the plain write to payload before the store to ready. The compiler may reorder the two stores, and on weakly ordered CPUs a consumer can see ready == true with a stale payload. The x86 hardware model rarely shows this, which is why the run passed. TSan flags it. Fix: release store and acquire load, as in the previous card.
Interview trap: 'it works on my laptop' tests the hardware, not the language guarantee.

front:
[Chain: MEMORDER 3/3] Context: the flag store defaults to memory_order_seq_cst. Compare the x86-64 that GCC emits for a release store and a seq_cst store. Why does the default cost more, and when do you actually need seq_cst?
#include <atomic>
std::atomic<int> x{0};
void store_release(int v) { x.store(v, std::memory_order_release); }
void store_seqcst(int v) { x.store(v, std::memory_order_seq_cst); }
back:
Headline: on x86 a seq_cst store needs a locked instruction, and a release store is a plain move.
Real GCC 13 -O2 output (the relevant lines):
_Z13store_releasei:
endbr64
movl	%edi, x(%rip)
ret
_Z12store_seqcsti:
endbr64
xchgl	x(%rip), %edi
ret
seq_cst requires all seq_cst operations to fit one total order, which on x86 needs the store to be globally ordered against later loads. GCC uses xchg, which is implicitly locked. Loads with seq_cst are plain moves on x86 (the usual mapping; not separately compiled here), so the extra cost sits on stores.
You need seq_cst for store-then-load patterns across two atomics (Dekker or Peterson-style mutual exclusion). Otherwise release/acquire is enough.
Where it breaks: do not generalise these x86 instructions. On other ISAs (for example AArch64) the seq_cst sequences differ; I did not compile for them here.

front:
Predict the output. What is the padding for, and what does the last line tell you about the target?
#include <atomic>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <new>
struct Naive { std::atomic<long> a{0}; std::atomic<long> b{0}; };
struct alignas(64) PaddedCounter { std::atomic<long> v{0}; };
struct Padded { PaddedCounter a; PaddedCounter b; };
int main() {
    std::cout << "Naive  size " << sizeof(Naive) << " alignof " << alignof(Naive) << "\n";
    std::cout << "Padded size " << sizeof(Padded) << " alignof " << alignof(Padded) << "\n";
    std::cout << "hardware_destructive_interference_size = "
              << std::hardware_destructive_interference_size << "\n";
}
back:
Headline: Naive packs two counters into 16 bytes, so both usually share one 64-byte line. Padded gives each counter its own line.
Real output:
Naive  size 16 alignof 8
Padded size 128 alignof 64
hardware_destructive_interference_size = 64
Two threads each writing their own Naive counter invalidate each other's cache line (false sharing). alignas(64) on PaddedCounter forces each counter to a full line, so Padded is 128 bytes. std::hardware_destructive_interference_size is a compile-time constant (64 on this target). GCC warns about its use in a header (-Winterference-size), because its value can change with flags across translation units.
Interview trap: 64 is the usual x86 line size, not a law. Some ARM designs use 128-byte lines (approx.; check the target).

GCC also warns that the returned future is ignored. The lines print in the order launching, slow body finished, after async statement, because the temporary future is destroyed (and waits) at the end of the expression statement.
Interview trap: keep the futures, or use std::jthread if you want fire-and-forget. Do not rely on async as detached work.

front:
Implement parallel_for(n, threads, body) with std::thread and static chunking, then use it to sum i squared for i below 1000. Show the code and output, and name its main cost.
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
template <class F>
void parallel_for(std::size_t n, unsigned threads, F&& body) {
    if (threads == 0) threads = 1;
    const std::size_t chunk = (n + threads - 1) / threads;
    std::vector<std::thread> pool;
    for (unsigned t = 0; t < threads; ++t) {
        const std::size_t lo = t * chunk, hi = std::min(n, lo + chunk);
        if (lo >= hi) break;
        pool.emplace_back([&body, lo, hi] {
            for (std::size_t i = lo; i < hi; ++i) body(i);
        });
    }
    for (auto& th : pool) th.join();
}
int main() {
    std::vector<double> out(1000);
    parallel_for(out.size(), 4, [&](std::size_t i) {
        out[i] = static_cast<double>(i) * static_cast<double>(i);
    });
    double s = 0;
    for (double x : out) s += x;
    std::cout << static_cast<long long>(s) << "\n";
}
back:
Check: the sum of i squared for i in 0..999 is (999)(1000)(1999)/6 = 332,833,500. Real output: 332833500.
The threads join before return, so the captured reference to body never dangles. The last chunk takes the remainder, and empty chunks are skipped.
Main cost: it creates and joins threads on every call. Production code uses a long-lived pool with a task queue; the thread creation cost then gets amortised.

front:
What is wrong with this thread-spawning loop? Give what three runs printed and the fix.
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
int main() {
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i)
        ts.emplace_back([&i] { std::cout << "worker " << i << "\n"; });
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
}
back:
Headline: [&i] captures the loop variable by reference. The loop keeps changing i while threads read it, which is a data race.
Real output:
worker 4 worker worker 4 4 worker 4
worker worker 44  worker 4 worker 4
worker worker worker 4 4 4 worker 4  (three runs)
The values are usually 4 (the value after the loop). Lines also interleave because std::cout is thread-safe per operation, not per statement. TSan reports: WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race.
Fix: capture by value ([i]) and collect results in a container that main prints after join:
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
int main() {
    std::vector<int> seen(4, -1);
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i)
        ts.emplace_back([i, &seen] { seen[i] = i; });   // i copied at creation
    for (auto& t : ts) t.join();
    for (int v : seen) std::cout << "worker " << v << "\n";
}

Real output:
worker 0
worker 1
worker 2
worker 3

Interview trap: the same bug appears with std::async and with pointers to loop-local variables.

The output order is deterministic here because the destructor runs at the closing brace and the worker sees the stop request before the join returns.
Interview trap: an unobservable infinite loop becomes a hang at scope exit, not a terminate. Plain std::thread would terminate in the same situation.

front:
What is wrong with this consumer? Compile it with -Wall -Wextra: does the compiler warn? Show the corrected wait and its output.
#include <condition_variable>
#include <mutex>
std::mutex m;
std::condition_variable cv;
bool ready = false;
int data = 0;
void consume() {
    std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m);
    cv.wait(lk);            // no predicate: returns on notify OR spurious wakeup
    int x = data;
    (void)x;
}
back:
Headline: the wait has no predicate. The compiler stays silent, which is why this bug survives code review.
Real compile result:
(no diagnostics; the compile succeeded)
Two defects: (1) condition_variable::wait may return spuriously, so after it returns the state must be checked; (2) the flag is never checked at all, so a notify sent before the wait started (a lost wakeup) leaves the thread blocked forever.
Fix: wait with a predicate, under the same mutex that guards the state:
cv.wait(lk, [] { return ready; });

Real output:
consumed 42

Interview trap: a condition_variable is a signal, not a flag. The predicate is the flag.

front:
Estimate pi with 4 threads, each doing 2,000,000 samples with its own generator seeded through std::seed_seq. Show the code and output, and name two caveats.
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <random>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
int main() {
    const int T = 4;
    const std::uint64_t N = 2000000;
    std::vector<std::uint64_t> hits(T, 0);
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < T; ++t) {
        ts.emplace_back([t, &hits] {
            std::seed_seq seq{20260101u, static_cast<unsigned>(t)};
            std::mt19937_64 rng(seq);
            std::uniform_real_distribution<double> U(0.0, 1.0);
            std::uint64_t h = 0;
            for (std::uint64_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
                const double x = U(rng), y = U(rng);
                if (x * x + y * y <= 1.0) ++h;
            }
            hits[t] = h;
        });
    }
    for (auto& th : ts) th.join();
    std::uint64_t total = 0;
    for (auto h : hits) total += h;
    std::printf("pi ~ %.6f\n", 4.0 * static_cast<double>(total) / static_cast<double>(T * N));
}
back:
Headline: one engine per thread, seeded from (base seed, thread id), with each thread writing its own result slot and the reduction after join.
Real output:
pi ~ 3.141749

Caveat 1: std::uniform_real_distribution is not required to produce the same sequence across standard libraries. For reproducible research, transform the raw 64-bit output yourself.
Caveat 2: never share one std::mt19937 across threads. That is a data race, and it serialises the work.

front:
Same Monte Carlo, but every thread uses std::mt19937_64 rng(12345). What do the outputs show, and what is the statistical consequence?
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <random>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
int main() {
    const int T = 4;
    const std::uint64_t N = 1000000;
    std::vector<std::uint64_t> hits(T, 0);
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < T; ++t) {
        ts.emplace_back([t, &hits] {
            std::mt19937_64 rng(12345);          // same seed in every thread
            std::uniform_real_distribution<double> U(0.0, 1.0);
            std::uint64_t h = 0;
            for (std::uint64_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
                const double x = U(rng), y = U(rng);
                if (x * x + y * y <= 1.0) ++h;
            }
            hits[t] = h;
        });
    }
    for (auto& th : ts) th.join();
    std::cout << "hits per thread: " << hits[0] << " " << hits[1] << " " << hits[2] << " " << hits[3] << "\n";
    std::cout << "all streams identical: " << std::boolalpha << (hits[0] == hits[1] && hits[1] == hits[2] && hits[2] == hits[3]) << "\n";
}
back:
Headline: the four streams are identical, so the four hit counts are one estimate counted four times.
Real output:
hits per thread: 785884 785884 785884 785884
all streams identical: true
With per-thread N = 106 samples, the combined estimate 4 x 785,884 / 4,000,000 = 3.143536 looks like 4 million samples, but it carries the information of 1 million. Standard error of one stream is 4 sqrt(p(1-p)/N) = 0.00164 (p = pi/4). With four independent streams the combined error would be 0.00082, so the identical-seed error is sqrt(4) = 2 times too large, and you believe it is smaller than it is.
Interview trap: the same seed on every process, node or GPU block gives this failure silently. Check that the streams differ, for example by comparing their first draws.

front: [Chain: RNG 1/3] Context: four threads of Monte Carlo pricing need statistically independent random streams. What is the minimum correct design with the C++20 standard library, and what does it not guarantee?
back:
Design: one engine per thread, never shared. Seed each with std::seed_seq built from (base seed, thread id). Each thread writes its own result slot, and the reduction happens after join (pi card above).
Not guaranteed: that the four sequences do not overlap or are uncorrelated. The standard gives you an engine and a seeding function, not a way to split a stream into provably disjoint parts.
Interviewer follow-up: 'Is a different integer seed per thread enough?' (Next card.)

front: [Chain: RNG 2/3] Context: each thread builds std::mt19937_64 rng(t) with t = 0, 1, 2, 3. Why is this not a guarantee of independent streams, and what does std::seed_seq change?
back:
Why not: the seed only selects an initial state. For mt19937 the 19,937-bit state moves along one very long cycle, and the standard specifies the algorithm but not where a given seed lands on that cycle. Two streams can therefore overlap or correlate in principle, and the standard gives you no way to check.
What seed_seq changes: it mixes all the words of its inputs into the initial state, so consecutive integer seeds land on very different states. This is a heuristic that greatly reduces the risk; it is still not a proof of non-overlap.
Interviewer follow-up: 'How would you guarantee disjoint streams?' Use a generator with a documented jump or a counter-based design (last card).
Where it breaks: in a distributed run, the seeds must come from one place (a master seed plus a unique stream index), not from the clock.

front: [Chain: RNG 3/3] Context: thread 7 must start its stream at draw number 250 of a shared sequence and draw 240 numbers. Can std::mt19937_64 do this efficiently with the standard interface? Work the cost and name the alternatives.
back:
Cost: discard(z) is specified as calling operator() z times, so it is O(z). Skipping 250 draws at an assumed 109 draws per second takes 13.0 days per thread (approx.). It is not an option.
Alternatives: (a) a counter-based generator (for example Philox from Random123): each output is a function of (key, counter), so a stream is a key and any offset costs O(1). (b) xoshiro256**, whose documented jump() advances the state by 2128 steps, so giving each thread its own jumped copy gives non-overlapping blocks (per the Blackman and Vigna reference; not re-verified here).
Interview trap: none of these is in the C++ standard library. A hand-rolled generator needs statistical tests (for example TestU01 or PractRand) before anyone trusts a Monte Carlo result from it.

front:
What is sizeof(OptAoS), and what does the spot loop touch? Predict the output, then explain the cache cost of AoS against SoA.
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
struct OptAoS { double spot, strike, vol, t; };
struct OptsSoA { std::vector<double> spot, strike, vol, t; };
double sum_spot_aos(const std::vector<OptAoS>& v) {
    double s = 0;
    for (const auto& o : v) s += o.spot;
    return s;
}
double sum_spot_soa(const OptsSoA& v) {
    double s = 0;
    for (double x : v.spot) s += x;
    return s;
}
int main() {
    const std::size_t N = 1000;
    std::vector<OptAoS> a(N);
    OptsSoA b;
    b.spot.resize(N);
    b.strike.assign(N, 1.0);
    b.vol.assign(N, 0.2);
    b.t.assign(N, 1.0);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        a[i] = {static_cast<double>(i), 1.0, 0.2, 1.0};
        b.spot[i] = static_cast<double>(i);
    }
    std::cout << "sizeof(OptAoS) = " << sizeof(OptAoS) << "\n";
    std::cout << "AoS sum spot = " << sum_spot_aos(a) << "\n";
    std::cout << "SoA sum spot = " << sum_spot_soa(b) << "\n";
}
back:
Headline: a 32-byte record, and the loop reads 8 of those bytes.
Real output:
sizeof(OptAoS) = 32
AoS sum spot = 499500
SoA sum spot = 499500
A 64-byte line holds two records, so the AoS spot loop pulls every line but uses 8 of its 32 bytes per record: 25 percent of each line is useful. SoA packs eight spots per line, and every byte pulled is used. The sums agree; only the memory traffic differs.
Interview trap: SoA hurts when the code needs every field of one option at a time, for example random access by option id. Blocked AoSoA layouts are the usual middle ground for SIMD.

front: Case study. A portfolio has 10 million options, stored as a 32-byte AoS record {spot, strike, vol, t}. A risk loop reads only spot. Compare the bytes pulled from memory per pass for AoS and SoA, the time at an assumed sustained bandwidth of 20 GB/s, the speedup, and a sanity check.
back:
Working. AoS: every 64-byte line is fetched because it holds two records, so the pass moves 107 x 32 bytes = 320 MB. SoA: only the spot array is read, 107 x 8 bytes = 80 MB. Ratio = 4x. At 20 GB/s (assumed), AoS takes about 16 ms and SoA about 4 ms (approx.).
Sanity check: the ratio equals record size over field size (32 / 8 = 4), independent of the bandwidth assumed. If the array fits in last-level cache, the traffic argument weakens and the compute and vector width matter more; measure with the real size.
Interviewer follow-up: 'When does AoS win?' When one pricer needs all four fields of one option at once.

front:
Compile these two saxpy loops at -O2 and at -O3 with -fopt-info-vec-optimized. What does the report say, and what does __restrict change?
void saxpy_restrict(float* __restrict y, const float* __restrict x, float a, int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i];
}
void saxpy_alias(float* y, const float* x, float a, int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i];
}
back:
Headline: with GCC 13, -O2 vectorised neither loop; -O3 vectorised both.
Real compiler reports:
-O2: (no vectorisation reported)
-O3: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Claude/20a381c2-80c6-5341-ac08-6b3c37d60a6d/scratchpad/work/17_cpp_m6/src/vec_saxpy.cpp:2:23: optimized: loop vectorized using 16 byte vectors

/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Claude/20a381c2-80c6-5341-ac08-6b3c37d60a6d/scratchpad/work/17_cpp_m6/src/vec_saxpy.cpp:5:23: optimized:  loop versioned for vectorization because of possible aliasing

The -O3 report shows the second loop gets a runtime aliasing check: the compiler versions the loop and chooses vector or scalar code at run time. __restrict asserts that the pointers do not alias, so no check is needed. The -O2 result follows GCC 13's cost model for this loop shape (not re-derived here).

front:
Count the 256-bit (ymm) instructions in the assembly for this dot product: default -O3, then -O3 with -march=native. What does -march=native change, and what is the deployment trap?
double dot(const double* a, const double* b, int n) {
    double s = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) s += a[i] * b[i];
    return s;
}
back:
Real counts (this host): default -O3: 0 ymm lines. -O3 -march=native: 4 ymm lines, and 1 vfmadd (fused multiply-add) instruction(s).
GCC reports -march=native as sapphirerapids on this machine. The default x86-64 target has no AVX, so it uses 128-bit xmm registers only.
Explanation: -march=native enables every extension the build host supports, and GCC then uses them where it judges them profitable; by default GCC prefers 256-bit vectors (-mprefer-vector-width=256), even on a CPU with 512-bit units.
Interview trap: a binary built with -march=native can fail with SIGILL on an older CPU. For a known fleet, use an explicit baseline such as -march=x86-64-v3 (AVX2, FMA).

front:
The operator new below counts allocations. Predict the two counts and explain the cost of the first loop.
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <iostream>
#include <new>
#include <vector>
static long long g_allocs = 0;
void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    ++g_allocs;
    if (void* p = std::malloc(n)) return p;
    throw std::bad_alloc{};
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }
__attribute__((noinline)) double payoff_bad(int i) {
    std::vector<double> path(8, static_cast<double>(i));
    return path.back();
}
__attribute__((noinline)) double payoff_good(int i, std::vector<double>& buf) {
    buf.assign(8, static_cast<double>(i));
    return buf.back();
}
int main() {
    double s = 0;
    long long before = g_allocs;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) s += payoff_bad(i);
    std::cout << "allocations, new vector per call: " << g_allocs - before << "\n";
    std::vector<double> buf;
    buf.reserve(8);
    before = g_allocs;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) s += payoff_good(i, buf);
    std::cout << "allocations, reused buffer:      " << g_allocs - before << "\n";
    std::cout << "checksum " << s << "\n";
}
back:
Headline: 1,000 heap allocations for a fresh vector per call, and none when the buffer is reused.
Real output:
allocations, new vector per call: 1000
allocations, reused buffer:      0
checksum 999000
Each payoff call constructs a std::vector, which allocates on the heap and frees on return. A hot loop with that pattern pays for malloc, free and cache misses on every iteration. The fix is a buffer owned outside the loop (reserve once), or a fixed std::array when the size is a compile-time constant. Both functions are marked noinline, and the non-zero count for the first loop shows the allocations survived optimisation in this build.
Interview trap: a benchmark that allocates nothing may just have had its work removed. Check the count or the assembly.

front:
Predict the allocation counts for a small and a large std::function capture. What decides the difference, and what should a latency-critical hot path use instead?
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdlib>
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <new>
static long long g_allocs = 0;
void* operator new(std::size_t n) {
    ++g_allocs;
    if (void* p = std::malloc(n)) return p;
    throw std::bad_alloc{};
}
void operator delete(void* p) noexcept { std::free(p); }
void operator delete(void* p, std::size_t) noexcept { std::free(p); }
int main() {
    double a[4] = {1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0};
    long long before = g_allocs;
    std::function<double()> small = [x = 1.5] { return x; };
    std::cout << "small capture (8 bytes): " << (g_allocs - before) << " allocation(s)\n";
    before = g_allocs;
    std::function<double()> big = [a] { return a[0] + a[1] + a[2] + a[3]; };
    std::cout << "big capture (32 bytes):  " << (g_allocs - before) << " allocation(s)\n";
    std::cout << small() + big() << "\n";
}
back:
Headline: the small capture stays inline; the 32-byte capture is heap allocated.
Real output:
small capture (8 bytes): 0 allocation(s)
big capture (32 bytes):  1 allocation(s)
11.5
libstdc++ stores small callables in an inline buffer (about two pointers, 16 bytes; implementation detail). Above that the wrapper allocates. Even inline, a std::function call is an indirect call through a type-erased pointer. In a latency-critical loop use a template parameter for the callable, so the compiler can inline it.
Interview trap: the buffer size is not part of the standard, so a test on one toolchain does not guarantee the behaviour on another.

front:
This 'benchmark' calls sum_recip(100000000) three times and discards the result. What is wrong, and what does the generated code show?
#include <iostream>
double sum_recip(int n) {
    double s = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) s += 1.0 / i;
    return s;
}
int main() {
    for (int r = 0; r < 3; ++r) sum_recip(100000000);
    std::cout << "benchmark done\n";
}
back:
Headline: the compiler removed the work, so the benchmark timed nothing.
Real output:
benchmark done
Evidence from the -O2 assembly: main contains no divsd (no division at all). The sum is pure and unused, so the loop disappears. With the result stored to a volatile sink, the division remains: divsd present.
Fix: store the result to a volatile sink, or use an empty asm with a memory clobber, as in Google Benchmark's DoNotOptimize, to make the value escape.
Interview trap: a benchmark that is suspiciously fast is dead code until shown otherwise. Look at the assembly.

front:
Both loops compute the sum of values at least 128. Predict the output for the unsorted and sorted data, then explain why sorting makes the branchy loop faster and what trap applies to measuring it.
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <random>
#include <vector>
long long sum_if(const std::vector<int>& v) {
    long long s = 0;
    for (int x : v) if (x >= 128) s += x;
    return s;
}
long long sum_branchless(const std::vector<int>& v) {
    long long s = 0;
    for (int x : v) s += (x >= 128) ? x : 0;
    return s;
}
int main() {
    std::mt19937 g(1);
    std::uniform_int_distribution<int> d(0, 255);
    std::vector<int> v(1 << 20);
    for (auto& x : v) x = d(g);
    std::cout << "unsorted: " << sum_if(v) << " " << sum_branchless(v) << "\n";
    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());
    std::cout << "sorted:   " << sum_if(v) << " " << sum_branchless(v) << "\n";
}
back:
Headline: the sums agree, so the sums prove correctness, not speed.
Real output:
unsorted: 100462251 100462251
sorted:   100462251 100462251
On random data the branch x >= 128 is true about half the time, so the predictor fails often. Sorted data gives long runs of one outcome, so the predictor is almost always right.
Trap: the compiler may turn either loop into conditional moves or vector code, which removes the branch and erases the sorted-versus-unsorted gap. Read the assembly before claiming a branch effect, and measure with realistic data.

front:
Both loops sum the same 2000 x 2000 matrix. Which is faster and why? Predict the printed sums, then say what the printed output does not tell you.
#include <cstddef>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
int main() {
    const std::size_t R = 2000, C = 2000;
    std::vector<double> M(R * C);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < R * C; ++i) M[i] = static_cast<double>(i % 97);
    double row_major = 0, col_major = 0;
    for (std::size_t r = 0; r < R; ++r)
        for (std::size_t c = 0; c < C; ++c) row_major += M[r * C + c];
    for (std::size_t c = 0; c < C; ++c)
        for (std::size_t r = 0; r < R; ++r) col_major += M[r * C + c];
    std::cout << "row-major sum " << static_cast<long long>(row_major) << "\n";
    std::cout << "col-major sum " << static_cast<long long>(col_major) << "\n";
}
back:
Headline: the row-major loop is the faster one on real hardware, and the printed sums are identical.
Real output:
row-major sum 191999527
col-major sum 191999527
The matrix is 32 MB, which normally exceeds the cache. The row loop walks contiguous memory, so every fetched line is fully used and the prefetcher works. The column loop strides 16,000 bytes, so each access touches a new line and usually a new page.
What the output does not show: the speed. Identical sums prove only that the loops do the same arithmetic. Time them at the production size, not at -O0.

front:
Implement an atomic maximum for non-negative doubles using compare_exchange_weak, since std::atomic has no fetch_max for double in C++20. Show the code and output, and say why relaxed ordering suffices here.
#include <atomic>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstring>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
std::atomic<std::uint64_t> best{0};
// Valid for x >= 0: IEEE-754 bit patterns of non-negative doubles order like integers.
void update_max(double x) {
    std::uint64_t bits;
    std::memcpy(&bits, &x, sizeof bits);
    std::uint64_t cur = best.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
    while (bits > cur &&
           !best.compare_exchange_weak(cur, bits, std::memory_order_relaxed, std::memory_order_relaxed)) {
    }
}
int main() {
    std::vector<std::thread> ts;
    for (int t = 0; t < 4; ++t)
        ts.emplace_back([t] { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) update_max(static_cast<double>(t * 1000 + i) * 0.5); });
    for (auto& th : ts) th.join();
    std::uint64_t b = best.load();
    double m;
    std::memcpy(&m, &b, sizeof m);
    std::cout << m << "\n";
}
back:
Trick: the IEEE-754 bit patterns of non-negative doubles order the same way as unsigned integers, so the CAS loop can compare the raw 64-bit patterns.
Real output:
1999.5
Relaxed suffices because there is one atomic location and the result is read after join, which gives a happens-before edge. No other data depends on the ordering.
Interview trap: negative values need a sign-flip transform, and NaN handling is separate. The loop is correct only for x >= 0 as written.

front: Derivation. Derive Amdahl's law for a fixed-size problem with serial fraction s on N cores. Compute the speedup at N = 8 and N = 16 for s = 0.05, the limit, and the scaled-workload (Gustafson) figure at N = 8. Where does the law break in a pricing loop?
back:
Derivation. Let the one-core time be T, split into a serial part sT that does not shrink and a parallel part (1-s)T that is divided evenly across N cores (a balanced-load assumption). Then T(N) = sT + (1-s)T/N, and S(N) = T/T(N) = 1 / (s + (1-s)/N). As N grows the second term vanishes, so S(N) tends to 1/s.
Numbers (python-checked): s = 0.05. S(8) = 5.93; S(16) = 9.14; S(64) = 15.42; the limit is 1/0.05 = 20.
Gustafson (scaled workload, serial part fixed, parallel part grows with N): S = N - s(N-1) = 7.65 at N = 8. The two laws answer different questions; the first fixes the problem size, the second fixes the time budget.
Where it breaks: (1) the serial fraction is not fixed: lock contention, false sharing and allocator locks add serial-like work that grows with N; (2) the parallel part is not balanced across cores, so the slowest core sets the time; (3) memory bandwidth is shared, so the parallel part does not scale past the bandwidth ceiling.

front: Derivation and case. A Monte Carlo price is an average of N independent path payoffs with per-path standard deviation sigma. Derive the number of paths needed for standard error eps and the wall-clock time on P threads. Take sigma = 12, eps = 0.01, 50 microseconds per path on one core (assumed), and 8 threads at 75 percent parallel efficiency (assumed).
back:
Derivation. By independence, Var(mean) = sigma^2 / N, so SE = sigma / sqrt(N). Requiring SE = eps gives N = (sigma/eps)^2.
Numbers (python-checked): N = (12 / 0.01)^2 = 1,440,000 paths. One core needs 1,440,000 x 50 microseconds = 72 s. With 8 threads at 75 percent efficiency the effective speedup is 6, so the wall time is 72 / 6 = 12 s (approx.). Halving eps quadruples N, because N is proportional to 1/eps^2.
Where it breaks: (1) identical or correlated streams cut the effective sample size, as shown by the identical-seed card: the error is sqrt(T) too large; (2) path cost varies, so a static split leaves cores idle; use dynamic chunks; (3) the 75 percent efficiency is an assumption, to be replaced by a measurement; (4) floating-point reductions in a different order change the last bits of the answer.

front: How do you profile a C++ hot loop with perf before optimising it? Give the commands, what to read in them, and the trap.
back:
Measure first: perf stat -e cycles,instructions,branch-misses,cache-misses ./prog. The key ratio is IPC = instructions / cycles: low IPC with many cache misses points at memory, low IPC with many branch misses points at prediction.
Find the hot code: perf record -g ./prog, then perf report. For useful stacks, build with -g and -fno-omit-frame-pointer (or record with --call-graph dwarf). perf annotate shows the hot instructions.
Trap: sampling skids, so the reported instruction can be a few instructions after the real cause. Profile a realistic input, and read the assembly of the reported function before editing.
Not run here: perf is not installed on this host, so these commands and flags were written from perf's documentation and not executed.

front: Hot-path rules of thumb: avoid {{c1::heap allocation}} (use buffers owned outside the loop), avoid {{c2::std::endl}} (it flushes the stream on every call), and avoid many cores writing one {{c3::shared atomic}} (its cache line moves between them).
back: Each rule is a hypothesis, not a law. Confirm with a profile (perf card), the allocation count (heap card), and the assembly. Related cards: heap allocation, std::function captures, false sharing, and the mutex chain.
